examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/819e3b9672e898801ef7320c1d80246d218ae89e76b3247c86b642a5f5790400.png)
Consider the system of linear ODEs $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for this system.
examples.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system $\mathbf x'(t) = A\mathbf x(t),$ denoted $\Phi_0(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
\Phi_0'(t) = A\Phi_0(t), \quad \Phi_0(0)  = I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that $\Phi_0(t) = e^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & -7 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & -7{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda) = \alpha_1 \lambda + \alpha_0.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
\lambda_1 = 7\textrm{i}t, \qquad
\lambda_2 = -7\textrm{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((7\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(7\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(7\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+7\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_0$ into the expressions for the required entries of $e^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(7t) \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t & =7\cdot \frac{1}{7t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(7t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

feedback.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$
